newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian conservatives angered by "culture invasion".
newsitem.headline: Indian conservatives angered by "culture invasion".

text.p: Political and religious groups in India are venting their wrath against the Miss World beauty pageant, singer Michael Jackson, fast food and a home-grown artist in a conservative backlash.
Indian newspapers were littered last week with reports of protests by activists in a rearguard action against a perceived Western cultural invasion.
Effigies of nationally celebrated artist M.F. Husain were burned in two states and a gallery showing his works was vandalised and some of his paintings were destroyed.
India's most popular film star, Amitabh Bachchan, had his effigy burned for helping to bring the Miss World beauty contest to India next month.
The Pizza Hut fast food restaurant in Bangalore was stoned again last week.
And the Hindu nationalist Swadeshi Jagaran Manch (SJM) pressure group put both Miss World and Michael Jackson on its unwanted list.
The disparate objects of ire change weekly but the theme is the same in a deeply rooted conservative culture trying to embrace liberal economic reform.
Husain, a mainly contemporary painter, has been the prime target recently.
The Moslem artist issued an apology on Friday, saying he had not wanted his painting of a naked Hindu goddess to upset the sensibilities of members of India's religious majority.

Miss World organisers on Saturday announced a strategic retreat by deciding to stage the swimsuit phase of the pageant in the Seychelles rather than risk inflaming Indian emotions with half-dressed women.
Although marginal to the main political debate, the issues have the advantage for opportunist politicans of being novel and highly visible.

They prick the sensitivities of a constituency being wooed by the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which promotes Hindu nationalism, and the Shiv Sena, its more ultra-conservative cousin based in Maharashtra state, political commentators said.

That was evident this week, they said, when the Bombay police, encouraged by Shiv Sena and BJP politicians, filed a charge against Husain for depicting the goddess in a way that offended religious feelings.
India's newspapers generally have supported Husain's right to paint what he wants, calling for reason and tolerance.

The Times of India headed one of its editorials last week with the words of America's assassinated president John F. Kennedy: "In a free society art is not a weapon... Artists are not the engineers of the soul".

That quote, which overturns Russian dictator Stalin's description of writers as the engineers of human souls, holds poignancy in a country priding itself in being the world's largest democracy, although it listed towards the Soviet Union during the Cold War years.
The police chief of Bangalore, site of the Miss World contest, is taking no chances with local hot-heads.
With an eye on an expected two billion television viewers, he said a crack commando team would be deployed along with 1,000 police to stop any militant action from spoiling the spectacle.
Bangalore already has had a taste of militant action.
Kentucky Fried Chicken and Pizza Hut restaurants there have been attacked by members of the populist Farmers Association, which has also threatened to torch the Miss World venue.
McDonald's burger chain opened its first outlet in India on Sunday. Realising the ubiquitous "Big Mac" would stick in some Indians throats, it is offering the non-beef "Maharaja Mac".
There were no reported protests at the opening in New Delhi.
